newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Port Arthur staff try to put massacre behind them.
newsitem.headline: Port Arthur staff try to put massacre behind them.

text.p: Traumatised staff at Australia's historic Port Arthur are piecing together their shattered lives and most are now back at work among the convict ruins where 35 people were shot dead last April.

Management of the tourist spot, on the rugged southeast coast of the island state of Tasmania, make only one request of visitors -- that they not speak to staff of the latest chapter in the old penal colony's brutal history.

"This event has touched us all and causes us all great pain," reads a small plaque erected two weeks ago at the entrance to the site where on April 28 a local misfit called Martin Bryant unleashed modern Australia's worst mass murder.

Bryant, who confessed to the murders early this month, was sentenced in the Tasmanian Supreme Court on Friday to be jailed for the "term of his natural life". The judge called him an intellectually retarded, pathetic social misfit.
The plaque is one of several stark reminders here of what judge William Cox described as a "chilling catalogue of crime".

A crude wooden cross hewn from ancient pine, bearing the names of the dead, stands in a pile of flowers on the foreshore. The site's Broad Arrow cafe, where 20 were gunned down within two minutes, is locked shut and its windows painted over.
Small holes have been scratched from morbid curiosity in the paint obscuring the cafe windows, and staff, though back at work, become distressed at the mention of April 28 by visitors.
"It was just getting too much," said Michael Langley, who was appointed after the massacre to head up a special management team, explaining why the plaque was erected.

Some staff now guiding tourists around the remote site, established in 1830 by British colonisers as a convict settlement for hardened criminals, were wounded in the murderous rampage and saw friends mercilessly shot dead.
"The majority are back there and I am very proud of the people (there)," said Vicki Skeggs, a staff member whose aunt, Janette Quin, was murdered in the Port Arthur site's car park.
Bryant, said by psychiatrists to be completely unable to understand the feelings of others, shot Quin once in the buttocks then finished her off with a shot in the back.

"What do you do if you don't go back to work. Do you sit at home and dwell on it? The relative and friends I lost would not have forgiven me if I didn't go back to work and get on with my life," Skeggs said.
"The doors are open and we're ready for people to come back and visit us. We have a smile for everyone....We just want to get on with our life as normal."
Brigid Cook, wounded as she tried to warn others to take cover, admits it has been difficult to return to work. But she says she will not let Bryant rob her of the rest of her life.
"I think you just endure difficulties some time if you want something desperately," Cook said. Asked what this was, she replied: "My life back."
Tourists wandering the quiet paths winding around the Port Arthur ruins, where convicts were once publicly flogged, also appreciate the local community's desire to return to normality.

"I think it was to sort of help people to come to terms with things," said visitor Lee Cannon, telling Reuters why she and her husband, Frank, had travelled here for a holiday from their home state of Queensland.
"If people don't come here, then the whole area is going to get bad vibes."
A demolition crew will begin here early next month to demolish the cafe but will leave some ruins behind to be used to erect a permanent memorial, site manager Langley told Reuters.
But for the moment, grieving family and friends, massacre survivors and tourists stand in quiet reflection at the simple wooden cross overlooking Port Arthur's harbour.

Among the bouquets strewn at the foot of the cross are some white and pink carnations from Carolyn Loughton, who saw her daughter killed in the cafe on April 28 as Bryant walked from table to table, laughing and shooting people in the head.
"To my beautiful daughter, Sarah Kate Loughton, who was murdered here....You are eternally with me, love mummy. R.I.P. my love."
